summary: Describes the ONC Remote Procedure Call version 2 protocol as it was deployed and accepted at the time. It lets a program call a procedure on another machine across the network. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 5531.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for one computer to ask another to do a job and send back the answer, as if the job were done locally.

questions: how does remote procedure call version 2 work
subtitle: A protocol that lets one computer ask another to run a function and get back the result.

tldr.problem: Programs on different machines need to call each other's functions, not just exchange data. It should feel like calling a local function, even though the work happens remotely.
tldr.mechanism: ONC RPC sends a message identifying the remote program, procedure, and arguments. The server receives it, runs the procedure, and sends back the results. The RPC protocol handles message format, versioning, error codes, and optional authentication.
tldr.outcome: ONC RPC became the de facto standard for distributed computing in Unix. It powers NFS, NIS, and many other services. The protocol is transport-independent and works on UDP or TCP. RFC 1831 was replaced by RFC 5531.

today: RFC 1831 was replaced by RFC 5531, which clarifies and standardizes ONC RPC for the modern Internet. ONC RPC remains in use in NFS, NIS, and other network services.

sections.title: The RPC Model
sections.content:
The Remote Procedure Call (RPC) model mimics how you call a function in the same program. The caller provides arguments, the callee runs the function and computes results, and control returns with the answer. In ONC RPC, the caller and callee are on different machines connected by a network.

The local model is simple: you place arguments in a known location (like a register), transfer control to the function, and the function returns control with results in the same location. RPC replicates this across the network: the client sends a message containing the procedure name and arguments, waits for the server's reply, and extracts the results when the reply arrives.

A key difference from local calls is that the server and client run asynchronously. The client blocks waiting for a reply, and the server processes one request at a time (or spawns threads for concurrency). Network failures, timeouts, and retransmissions are possible and must be handled by the application.
sections.plainLanguage: In a program, you call a function by name with arguments, and it gives you back a result. RPC does the same, but the function runs on another computer.

sections.title: Programs, Procedures, and Versions
sections.content:
RPC terminology distinguishes several levels. A program is a set of procedures running on a server (like a file service). Each program has a unique program number, assigned by a central registry (rpc@sun.com). Within a program, each procedure has a number (e.g., "read" is procedure 3, "write" is procedure 4). Each program also has a version number to support protocol evolution. Servers can implement multiple versions of the same program for backward compatibility.

For example, the "NFS" file service might be program number 100003 with versions 2 and 3 both available. A client connecting to version 2 gets the old protocol, while a client connecting to version 3 gets new features.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs have numbers, procedures within them have numbers, and each program can have multiple versions. This lets old and new clients use the same server.

sections.title: The RPC Message Protocol
sections.content:
All RPC messages start with a transaction ID (xid) that identifies the call-reply pair. Then comes the message type: either CALL (from client) or REPLY (from server). In a CALL message, the client specifies the program number, program version, procedure number, authentication credentials, and procedure parameters. In a REPLY message, the server sends a response status and results (or an error explanation).

A reply can be ACCEPTED or DENIED. If accepted, the server provides the procedure results or an error code (PROG_UNAVAIL, PROC_UNAVAIL, GARBAGE_ARGS, etc.). If denied, the server says why: either the RPC version is unsupported or the client failed authentication. All messages include authentication verifiers to identify the caller and server.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has a tracking number, a direction (request or reply), and identifies which procedure to call or which result to send back.

sections.title: Authentication and Credentials
sections.content:
RPC defines an authentication flavor field and opaque authentication data in both calls and replies. Flavors include AUTH_NONE (no authentication), AUTH_SYS (Unix user ID and group ID), and AUTH_SHORT (a shorthand credential issued by the server). The RPC protocol allows for expansion: developers can define new flavors by applying to rpc@sun.com for a flavor number.

In AUTH_SYS, the client sends a timestamp, machine name, user ID, group ID, and list of supplementary groups. The server receives this and decides whether to execute the request. AUTH_SYS is not secure—it relies on the assumption that privileged network ports are only available to authorized users. For stronger security, mechanisms like Kerberos can be layered on top of RPC.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC can check who is making the request. AUTH_NONE means anyone, AUTH_SYS sends the Unix user ID. More secure methods are possible too.

sections.title: Transports and Reliability
sections.content:
RPC is transport-independent. It can run on UDP (an unreliable datagram protocol) or TCP (a reliable stream protocol). On UDP, the application must handle timeouts and retransmissions. If the client retransmits and the server already executed the request, the client cannot tell how many times the procedure actually ran. Servers can use the transaction ID to detect and suppress duplicate requests, providing "at-most-once" semantics.

On TCP, the connection handles retransmission automatically, so the application can infer that if a reply is received, the procedure executed exactly once. Even on TCP, timeouts are needed for server crashes. For efficiency, RPC on TCP uses record marking: a 4-byte header on each message indicates the message size and whether more data follows.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC works on fast but unreliable UDP or slow but reliable TCP. On TCP, you know the server got your request if you get a reply. On UDP, you might need to ask again.

sections.title: The RPC Language Definition
sections.content:
RPC includes a formal language to describe programs and their procedures, extending the XDR (eXternal Data Representation) language. A program declaration gives the program number and lists its versions. Each version declaration gives the version number and lists procedures. Each procedure declares its return type, name, parameter types, and procedure number.

For example, a ping program might declare: program PING_PROG { version PING_V1 { void PING(void) = 1; } = 1; } = 100000; This defines program 100000, version 1, with one procedure (PING) numbered 1 that takes no arguments and returns void. The language enables automatic code generation for both client and server stubs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a formal way to describe what procedures exist, what they take as input, what they return, and how to find them.
